elements.element: Customer has a right to terminate for convenience.
elements.evidence: The added language states that “Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience.”

elements.element: Customer may exercise its termination-for-convenience right on 30 days’ prior written notice to Vendor.
elements.evidence: The clause expressly requires “30 days’ prior written notice to Vendor.”

elements.element: Upon Customer’s termination for convenience, Vendor must provide a pro-rata refund of prepaid fees allocable to the period after termination becomes effective.
elements.evidence: Vendor must “refund any prepaid Fees for the period after the effective date of termination,” which provides the required pro-rata refund.

elements.element: Vendor has no termination-for-convenience right during a committed term.
elements.evidence: The clause states exactly that “Vendor has no right to terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience during a committed term.”

elements.element: Customer has a right to terminate for convenience.
elements.evidence: The added language grants Customer a right to terminate the Agreement or any Order Form for convenience.

elements.element: Customer’s termination-for-convenience right requires between 60 and 90 days’ notice.
elements.evidence: The clause requires only 30 days’ prior written notice, which is below the fallback range.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee imposed on Customer does not exceed three months’ fees.
elements.evidence: The clause imposes no early-termination fee, so the condition for applying the cap is demonstrably absent.
The clause does not affirmatively grant Vendor a termination-for-convenience right; it only denies such a right during a committed term.

elements.element: Any Vendor termination for convenience may become effective only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: The express prohibition on Vendor termination for convenience “during a committed term” prevents such termination from becoming effective before the term ends.

elements.element: Vendor must provide 90 days’ notice of any termination for convenience.
elements.evidence: No 90-day notice requirement applies to Vendor.

result.reason: The redline fully implements the preferred position: Customer receives a 30-day written-notice convenience right, post-termination prepaid fees are refunded, and Vendor has no such right during a committed term. It does not independently satisfy the fallback because Customer’s notice period is outside the 60–90-day range and Vendor is neither affirmatively granted an end-of-term convenience right nor subjected to 90 days’ notice. The changes are targeted and preserve the existing cause-based termination rights.
